newsitem.title: CHINA: APRIL's Riaupulp compromises in bond row.
newsitem.headline: APRIL's Riaupulp compromises in bond row.

text.p: Asia Pacific Resources Holdings (APRIL) subsidiary PT Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (Riaupulp) has tried to buy some good will by compromising on its Yankee bond buyback.
Riaupulp Finance Director Michael Verge said the new plan might cost the firm some money but that it would be worth it.
"I think it would be more costly not to come to a compromise with our bondholders," Verge told Reuters on Wednesday.

"These people invested in our company to begin with, and we certainly did not want to harm our reputation or injure our bondholders in any way. So, this is a nice compromise all the way around," he said.
Buying back the US$300 million in outstanding Yankee bonds would cost Riaupulp about US$318 million, he said.

The company announced on Tuesday it would purchase all outstanding 11 1/2 percent guaranteed secured notes due in 2000 and all 13 1/4 percent guaranteed secured notes due 2005 issued by its subsidiary RAPP International Finance Co BV.
Riaupulp said in January it would call the bonds at 101 percent of principal to satisfy a mandatory redemption triggered by its sale of two plants.
Bondholders were outraged by the call, claiming the redemption was not adequately described in the bond's circular and the plant sales that triggered it were unnecessary.
At that time of the call, the bonds were trading well above 101, with the 2000 bonds at 105 and the 2005 bonds at 111.

Under the new buyback scheme, Riaupulp is offering to buy the notes due 2000 at US$1,014 per US$1,000 principal amount plus accrued interest up to the payment date, with an additional US$20 per US$1,000 paid for consent by the holder to eliminate certain covenants.
For the notes due 2005, it is offering US$1,050 per US$1,000 principal plus accrued interest and an additional US$20 per US$1,000 for a similar consent.
The two features add up to a redemption price of 103.4 for the shorter-dated bond and 107 for the long bond.

Under the terms of the indenture, Riaupulp can strip many covenants from the bond that protect investors, such as the capital ratios the company must maintain and restrictions on its borrowing and lending, if 51 percent of the bonds are returned.
"That makes the alternative to the cash offer look a lot less attractive than the cash offer," said Verge.
Verge said the company has conferred with about 90 percent of the bondholders and expects most to accept the buyback plan.
The offers expire on August 11. Bear, Stearns and Co is acting as dealer manager.
Fund managers in Asia said they were pleased the bonds would be redeemed above the 101 call price, but they also said the wrangling over the deal had been a headache.
"It leaves a bad taste in your mouth," said one investor.
Most of the Yankee bonds are held by major institutional investors in the U.S., but Asian fund managers own some bonds.
"People have short memories so, I guess Riaupulp will come to the market again in a few years and everyone will buy the issue, having forgotten what happened," said another Asian investor.
There was one plus for RAPP paper holders, he said.
Because the paper was locked at the 101 call price for months, the paper did not widen as did other Asian credits in the wake of recent currency market volatility in the region.
"There were an awful lot of people that have saved a lot of money, given the volatility of the Indonesion market over the last couple of weeks," the fund manager said.
Verge said the company had no plans to tap the Yankee market again in the near future.
But it plans to raise US$300 million worth of rupiah bonds. Proceeds of the fixed-rate issue, which will have a maturity of five to seven years, will be used for plant expansion.
